items.title: Kant gave multiple formulations of the categorical imperative
items.claim: How does Kant's categorical imperative work?

options.text: One simple rule: do unto others as you would have them do to you

Multiple formulations including universalisability ('act only according to that maxim by which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law') and humanity-as-end ('act so as to treat humanity, whether in your own person or in that of another, always as an end, never as a means only')
Whatever maximises happiness is morally required
An empirical rule derived from observation

items.reveal:
Kant's 'Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals' (1785) sets out the categorical imperative. Standard count: three formulations.

Formula of Universal Law: 'Act only according to that maxim by which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.'
Formula of Humanity: 'Act so as to treat humanity, whether in your own person or in that of another, always as an end, never as a means only.'
Formula of the Kingdom of Ends: 'Act according to the maxims of a member of a merely possible kingdom of ends.'

The formulations are intended to be equivalent in extension but to emphasise different aspects. Kant's most famous example (lying to the murderer at the door) shows the strict reading: lying is universally impermissible.
items.why: Kantian ethics is sometimes reduced to 'don't lie' or 'universalise your action'. The multiple formulations and the humanity-as-end principle are richer — and more humane — than the slogan suggests.

items.title: The Torah is the first five books of the Hebrew Bible

options.text: The first five books — Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy — traditionally attributed to Moses; also called the Pentateuch or Chumash

items.reveal:
The Hebrew Bible (Tanakh) has three sections: Torah (Teaching, 5 books), Nevi'im (Prophets, 8 books), Ketuvim (Writings, 11 books). Tanakh is an acronym of those three.

The Torah is read in synagogue in a one-year cycle (annual cycle) or three-year cycle (some Reform congregations). The annual cycle ends and restarts on Simchat Torah.

The written Torah is complemented by the Oral Torah — the rabbinic tradition codified in the Mishnah (around 200 CE) and Talmud (around 500 CE). For Orthodox Judaism, both were revealed at Sinai.
items.why: 'The Torah' as a generic term for Jewish scripture obscures structure. Students need to distinguish Torah, Tanakh and Talmud — and notice that Christian 'Old Testament' is the same content as Tanakh but in different order.

items.title: The Torah is the first five books of the Hebrew Bible

options.text: The first five books — Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy — traditionally attributed to Moses; also called the Pentateuch or Chumash; the first section of the Hebrew Bible (Tanakh)

items.reveal:
The Hebrew Bible (Tanakh) is structured in three sections: Torah (Teaching, 5 books), Nevi'im (Prophets, 8 books in Jewish count), Ketuvim (Writings, 11 books). 'Tanakh' is an acronym of those three.

The Torah is read in synagogue in an annual cycle (some Reform congregations use a triennial cycle). The cycle ends and restarts on Simchat Torah.

The Written Torah is complemented by the Oral Torah — the rabbinic tradition codified in the Mishnah (around 200 CE) and Talmud (around 500 CE). For Orthodox Judaism, both were revealed at Sinai.
items.why: 'The Torah' is often used loosely. Students need to distinguish Torah (5 books) from Tanakh (24 books) from Talmud (rabbinic commentary) — and notice that the Christian Old Testament has the same content but in different order.
